summary: This unit teaches you to represent and promote a public body or other organisation: to know its mandate, services and brand; to speak with authority but only within your brief; to keep to the code of conduct and political neutrality; to prepare key messages and briefing notes; to follow protocol; to handle questions, the media and social media; to plan and run promotion such as a booth or outreach event; to take part in meetings and committees; and to report back and measure results.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. To **represent** an organisation is to speak and act in its name, for example at a community meeting, an inter-agency committee, a conference or on the telephone. To **promote** it is to make its services, aims and achievements known to the people who need them. At Level 5 you do both for a ministry, agency, municipal corporation, school, hotel or business, and you prepare and brief other staff to do the same.

In Jamaica the public sees the organisation through its officers. A courteous, well-informed officer builds trust; one careless answer, gift or social media post can damage a reputation that took years to build. For that reason this unit is about **preparation, authority, ethics and results** as much as it is about speaking well.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Know the organisation
Explain its mandate, mission, services, stakeholders and brand, and give a short, accurate summary of its work.
Represent it with authority and integrity
Stay within your brief, keep to the code of conduct, declare conflicts of interest, refuse improper gifts and stay politically neutral.
Prepare to represent
Prepare key messages, a briefing note and likely questions, and check protocol, titles and dress.
Communicate in public
Present clearly, answer questions honestly, deal with angry people, work with the media and use social media properly.
Plan and carry out promotion
Set aims, choose the audience, messages and channels, and run a booth, outreach event or campaign within budget.
Take part in meetings and committees
Present the organisation's position, listen, network and avoid commitments beyond your authority.
Report back and evaluate
Record outcomes and commitments, follow them up, and measure results with simple figures such as cost per enquiry.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, including short sums on percentages, cost per enquiry and budget shares.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as mandate, brand guidelines, conflict of interest) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** done in a group: plan and staff an information booth for a made-up public body, and represent the organisation at a meeting and write a report back.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms in the Revision section. Short answers ask for exact words such as mandate, spokesperson, outreach and political neutrality.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Knowing the organisation and its brand

blocks.p: You cannot represent what you do not know. Before you speak for an organisation, you must be able to explain, in plain words and without notes, what it is for, what it offers, to whom, and what it is trying to achieve now.

head: Item
What it means
Example (a parish municipal corporation)
rows: Mandate
The official purpose and powers of a public body, usually set by law or by the Government. It limits what the body may do.
To manage local roads, markets, public cleansing and local planning matters in the parish
Mission
A short statement of what the organisation does and for whom, today
We provide clean, safe and well-run public services to everyone in the parish
Vision
A picture of what the organisation wants to become or achieve in the long term
A clean, safe and prosperous parish
Core values
The standards of behaviour that guide staff
Integrity, respect, fairness, service
Services
What the public can get, and how to get it (steps, forms, fees, times, contacts)
Market stall licences, garbage collection schedule, building approvals
Current priorities
What the body is stressing this year, taken from its plan
A new recycling programme and market repairs
Stakeholders
People and groups with an interest in the body, or affected by it
Residents, vendors, councillors, ministries, donors, the media

blocks.p: A **mandate** is not the same as a mission. The mandate says what the body is **allowed and required** to do; the mission says how the body describes its purpose. A representative must never promise something outside the mandate.

blocks.h: Reputation and every officer as an ambassador

blocks.p: **Reputation** is how the public, partners and others see and judge the organisation. It is built mostly by experience: the officer at the counter, the voice on the telephone, the speed of a reply, the way a complaint is handled. A rude officer, a video that spreads online or a careless remark at a meeting can harm the reputation of the whole body.

For this reason **every member of staff is an ambassador**, not only the managers or the communications unit. Front-line staff are the people the public meets most, so they must understand the mission, know the main services, be courteous and know where to send a question they cannot answer.

**Corporate identity** is the look and voice of the organisation: its name, logo, colours, fonts, slogan and style of writing. **Brand guidelines** are the document that tells staff how these must be used. A consistent identity makes the body easy to recognise and trusted.

ul: Use the official logo supplied by the communications unit. Never stretch, recolour, redraw or crowd it.
Use the approved colours, fonts and templates for letters, flyers, posters, slides and web pages.
Use the approved name and contact details. Check telephone numbers and addresses every time.
If a unit wants a different design, it asks the communications unit. It does not invent its own.

blocks.p: An **elevator pitch** is a short, clear summary of the organisation that can be said in about 30 seconds. Use three parts: who we are, who we serve and what we offer, then one useful next step.

blocks.note: Example: "We are the parish's municipal corporation. We look after local roads, markets and garbage collection for everyone in the parish. This month we are starting a recycling programme; leaflets at the front desk explain how to take part."
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **citizens' charter** is a public promise by a public body about the standards of service the public can expect, for example how quickly a letter will be answered or a permit processed, and how to complain if the standard is not met. Know your body's charter, quote it accurately and never promise better than it says.

blocks.note: Jamaican public bodies often have a citizens' charter and a communications unit. Ask your own unit where the approved key messages, brand guidelines and charter are kept.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When you represent the organisation you carry its authority, but only as far as it has given it to you. You also carry the standards expected of every public officer. The most common ways in which representatives get into trouble are speaking beyond their brief, accepting a gift, hiding a conflict of interest and expressing a political opinion.

Your **brief** is the instruction from your manager about what you may say, agree to and commit the organisation to. To stay within the brief means to speak only on matters you are authorised to cover, to use the approved position, and to refer other matters back.

head: Situation
What a good representative does
rows: You are asked something you know and are authorised to answer
Answer clearly, accurately and briefly, using approved facts
You are asked about a decision that has not yet been made
Say that no decision has been made yet and that you will report the question back. Do not guess or hint
You are asked for a commitment (money, a date, a contract)
Say it is outside your authority, note the request and take it to the person who can decide
You are asked for your personal opinion
Say you are here to represent the organisation, and give the organisation's position
You do not know the answer
Say so. Take the person's name and contact details, promise a reply by a stated date, and keep the promise

blocks.note: Never guess. A wrong answer given in the organisation's name can mislead the public and be quoted back to you. "I will find out and reply by Friday" is a professional answer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **Political neutrality** means a public officer serves the Government of the day and the public fairly, whatever their own party views, and does not take sides in party politics while doing official work. In practice:

ul: Explain policies and services accurately without praising or attacking any party.
At a community meeting before an election, do not say which party's plan is better. Decline politely and return to the services the body provides.
Do not wear party colours or use official time, vehicles, premises or social media accounts for party activity.
Treat residents of every party with the same courtesy and the same service.

blocks.h: Code of conduct, gifts and conflicts of interest

blocks.p: A **code of conduct** sets the standards of behaviour expected of public officers: honesty, fairness, respect, proper use of resources and care with official information. It includes rules on gifts and on conflicts of interest. Follow your own body's code and ask your manager when in doubt.

head: Issue
What it means
What to do
rows: Gifts and hospitality
Offers of items, favours or entertainment from people who deal with, or want something from, the organisation

Decline politely, or follow the code's rule on declaring and recording it. A valuable gift such as an expensive watch is never accepted quietly. A small token such as a calendar may be allowed under the code
Conflict of interest
A situation where your private interests (family, friends, business) could affect, or seem to affect, your official duties
Declare it at once to your manager or the chair, and step aside from the decision. Do not try to balance it out by scoring the person lower or higher
Bribery and corruption
Asking for or taking money or favours to speed up or change a service

Never take part. If a member of the public reports that an officer asked for payment, take the details and report it through the proper channel. Do not challenge the officer in public, and do not advise the person to pay
Confidential information
Information not yet public, such as an unfinished contract negotiation, personal records or draft plans
Do not share it, hint at it or give it "off the record" to a friendly person. Say it cannot be discussed while talks are going on

blocks.note: The appearance of a conflict matters as much as the fact. If a reasonable person could think your judgement is affected, declare it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: When you collect names, telephone numbers or emails at a booth or meeting, the data protection law and your body's policy apply. Collect only what you need, tell people why, take it **only with consent**, keep it safe, and use it only for the stated purpose.

Promotion must be **truthful**. If a manager wants a poster to say that all permits are processed "in 24 hours" when most take five days, the officer preparing it should raise the concern and suggest a claim that is true, such as "most permits are processed within five working days". Misleading promises damage trust and lead to complaints.
Good representation is mostly done before the event. Use the steps below whenever you are asked to speak, attend or staff a stand for your body.

flow: Confirm the purpose, audience, date, place and your role
Get the brief: position, limits of authority, what you may and may not say
Gather facts and figures and check them with the right unit
Prepare key messages and a short opening
List likely questions and prepare approved answers
Check protocol, titles, dress and logistics
Rehearse, then travel early with your pack

blocks.p: When a director cannot attend a meeting and sends a deputy, the deputy must be briefed. A good **briefing note** is short (one to two pages) and contains:

head: Part
What it contains
rows: Purpose and context
What the event or meeting is, who is attending and why the body is involved
Background
A short history of the issue, with dates and figures
The body's position
The agreed position and the reasons for it, with any fallback already approved
Limits of authority
What the representative may agree to, and what must go back to the body
Key messages
Three to five points that the body wants the audience to take away
Likely questions and answers
Hard questions and the approved answers, with facts and contacts
Stakeholders
Who will be there, their interests and any history
Contacts and follow-up
Who to call for facts, who will take the notes, and when the report is due

blocks.p: A briefing pack for a conference might also include the programme, the venue map, business cards, flyers and the ministry's approved presentation. Irrelevant papers (for example, three years of the officer's own appraisal reports or every file on past conferences) only get in the way.

**Key messages** are the few clear points the organisation wants people to remember. They keep every officer giving the same accurate facts, and they stop different staff from contradicting each other. A good key message is short, true, in plain language and linked to what the audience cares about.

head: Weak message
Better message
rows: The Authority is committed to a paradigm shift in waste solutions
From 1 March, recyclables are collected every Tuesday. Use the blue bin.
We are the best agency in the region
Most permits are processed in five working days. Apply online or at any parish office.

blocks.p: **Protocol** is the accepted way of treating officials and guests at formal events. Getting it right shows respect and avoids embarrassment to your body.

ul: **Titles and forms of address:** in Jamaica, a Government Minister is introduced as "the Honourable" followed by the full name; a Mayor is addressed as "His Worship" or "Her Worship"; the Prime Minister and the Governor-General have their own styles. Check the correct title with the protocol officer, the ministry or the invitation, and never use a first name only on formal occasions.

**Order of precedence:** the accepted ranking in which dignitaries are introduced, seated and invited to speak. When several dignitaries attend, ask the ministry's protocol officer or use official guidance. Do not guess.

**Dress code:** check it on the invitation. For a formal function such as one at King's House, dress as the invitation says, normally formal or business dress. Casual clothes are not a way of seeming approachable.
**Punctuality and courtesy:** arrive early, introduce yourself, wear your identification, switch off your phone, thank the hosts and do not leave early.

blocks.note: If you are unsure of any title, ask beforehand. A short call to the protocol officer is far better than a wrong title said aloud.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Speaking, questions, the media and social media

blocks.p: Match the talk to the audience and the time. With 10 minutes for a group of farmers, choose **a few services that matter to farmers**, give an example, say how to get help and leave time for questions. Reading the annual report aloud, showing 40 slides of figures or using technical terms does not inform people.

ul: Open with who you are and why you are there. Give three main points. End with the next step and your contact.
Use plain language, short sentences and local examples. Explain any abbreviation.
Look at the audience, speak clearly and keep to time.

head: Situation
Best response
rows: Detailed question you cannot answer
Say you do not have the answer now, take the person's details, promise a reply by a date and keep it
Angry resident says complaints have been ignored
Stay calm, listen, accept the frustration without arguing or blaming, and offer a specific follow-up. Do not say it is someone else's responsibility or list what other agencies fail to do
Question outside the event's topic (for example water supply at a road safety event)
Record the concern and pass it to the right body. Do not ignore it, and do not promise a quick fix
Criticism from a donor or partner
Reply calmly with facts and refer policy points to the head of the body. Do not argue, agree that all has failed or walk out
Request to comment on a rumour about the organisation's budget
Do not confirm or deny. Say you are not the right person and refer them to the communications unit

blocks.p: Only authorised people speak to the media for the organisation. The **spokesperson** is the person authorised to speak to the media on its behalf, usually the head or the communications officer. Other officers should be polite and **refer journalists to the communications unit**. Never say anything "off the record", never confirm a rumour you cannot verify and never deny it when you do not know the facts.
When you are the spokesperson: agree the key messages first; answer the question you are asked, briefly and truthfully; say "I will find out" rather than guess; and do not give political opinions.

ul: Only officers **authorised by the communications policy** post on the official pages.
Official posts follow the brand guidelines, are accurate, respectful and in plain language.

On a personal page, do not present your views as the organisation's views. Do not post confidential information, photos of clients or records, or criticism of a Minister's policy. Even with a disclaimer, an officer's posts about work can be read as the organisation's view.
Reply to questions on official pages courteously and quickly. Move personal or complaint details to a private channel.

blocks.note: Before you post, ask: Is it true? Is it approved? Would I be content to see it on the front page, with my body's name on it?
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Promotion is planned like any other piece of work. Start with **what you want to achieve and with whom**, not with the decorations or the free items.

flow: Set aims (specific and measurable)
Identify the target audience
Agree the key messages
Choose channels and activities
Set the budget and timetable
Prepare materials and brief staff
Carry out, collect feedback
Evaluate and record lessons

blocks.h: Setting aims and choosing the audience

blocks.p: A good aim is measurable: "400 serious enquiries and 120 registrations started at the booth over three days" is clearer than "to raise awareness". The audience shapes everything. A recycling programme for residents needs different messages and channels from a grant for small businesses. A body should decide the **target audience and the message before it chooses the channels**.

head: Channel
Strengths
Limits
rows: Radio
Reaches many people, including rural and older people; good for short, repeated messages
Little detail; air time costs money
Social media
Cheap and fast; reaches younger and urban people; allows questions
Reaches fewer older people; comments must be monitored
Community meetings and outreach (markets, churches, schools)
Face-to-face explanation; builds trust
Reaches a limited number of people; takes staff time
Printed material (leaflets, posters)
Can be taken home; useful at counters and events
Costs to print; out of date quickly if details change
Website
Full detail, any time
Only people with internet and the skills to use it
Expos and trade shows
Meet many interested people in one place
Costs of booth and staff; needs good follow-up

blocks.p: A mix usually works best. For a recycling programme, demonstrations at markets and schools with simple leaflets reach residents better than a long technical report on a website or a notice in the staff newsletter. To reach both rural seniors and young urban workers, combine radio and community meetings with social media.

ul: **Accurate:** check every fact, date, number and contact before printing. Wrong details mislead the public and harm trust.
**Plain language:** short sentences, no jargon, the main point first.
**Accessible:** use more than one format and channel (print, radio, online, large print, sign language or help in person where needed) so that more citizens can reach and understand it.
**On brand:** follow the brand guidelines for logo, colours and fonts.
**Honest:** promise only what the body can deliver.

blocks.h: Running a booth at an expo or fair

ul: Name roles: booth manager, messages officer, materials, outreach (sign-up forms) and evaluation.
Keep the stand neat, safe (no loose cables) and staffed at all times, with breaks rostered.
Greet visitors, ask what they need, give the key message and one next step.
Collect contact details **only with consent**, and say what they will be used for.
Record every enquiry (a tally or form) so that you can measure results afterwards.

blocks.p: Share the budget among the activities in line with the aims. Work every sum twice.

blocks.note: Worked example: an agency has J$1,200,000 for a promotion. It plans 40% on radio, 35% on social media and the rest on printed material. Radio is J$480,000 (1,200,000 x 0.40); social media is J$420,000 (1,200,000 x 0.35); together J$900,000. Printed material = J$1,200,000 - J$900,000 = **J$300,000**. Check: 100% - 40% - 35% = 25% and 25% of J$1,200,000 = J$300,000.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A representative on a parish development committee or an inter-agency group works with other members repeatedly. Good relationships help the members work together and **settle issues early** before they become disputes. You do not befriend people to get favours, or to make the committee agree with you.

blocks.h: Representing the organisation at a meeting

flow: Read the agenda and papers; agree the position and limits with your director
Arrive early; introduce yourself and the body
Present the position clearly and accurately
Listen; take notes; ask questions
Refer matters beyond your authority back to the body
Record agreements and your own commitments
Report back and follow up

ul: **Do not commit** the body to costs, dates or actions beyond your authority. Say you will take it back and reply.
**Do not undermine** the body's position, even if you privately disagree. Raise concerns with your director beforehand.
**Vote in line with the body's agreed position** when you represent it on a committee. If the position is not clear, do not vote until you have asked.
If you agree to supply data by the end of the month, **record the promise, tell your manager and see that it is kept**.

blocks.p: **Networking** at a conference means building contacts that help the body meet its aims, for example a partner who could share training rooms or a supplier of data. Collecting as many business cards as possible is not the purpose. Follow up within a few days with a short, polite message.

Where a public meeting is about a disputed issue, such as a delayed road repair, prepare facts first: the reason for the delay, the new timetable and what the body can and cannot promise. At the meeting, state the purpose and ground rules (one person speaks at a time), acknowledge the inconvenience, apologise for the delay without blaming others, answer honestly, record every question and promise and say when residents will hear back.

After you have represented the body, **report outcomes, commitments and follow-up actions**. Do not keep the notes until someone asks, and do not share private discussions with colleagues over lunch or on social media.

head: Part of a back-to-office report
Contents
rows: Meeting details
Date, place, who attended, your role
Main points and outcomes
What was decided or agreed
Commitments
What the body promised, to whom and by when; what others promised
Issues and risks
Concerns raised, public feeling, risks to the body's reputation
Recommended follow-up
Actions, owners and dates; replies owed to people whose questions were not answered

blocks.p: Concerns raised outside your topic, for example complaints about water supply at a road safety event, are recorded and passed to the right body, and the resident is told that this has been done.

sections.title: Evaluating promotion and learning from it

blocks.p: Evaluation shows whether the money and time achieved the aim, and what to improve. The measure must match the aim.

head: Aim
Measure that shows it
rows: Recruit trainees at a careers fair
Number of applications received from the fair
Get serious enquiries at an expo
Number of serious enquiries recorded; cost per enquiry
Inform residents about a new service
Visitors reached, share of people who say the information was useful, change in service use
Improve the body's image
Share of media stories that are positive, feedback ratings

blocks.p: Numbers such as flyers printed, staff at the booth or photos posted online show activity, not results. Always ask: does this measure show whether the aim was met?

blocks.h: The sums you must be able to do

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: Cost per enquiry
Total cost / number of enquiries
Percentage of target
Actual / target x 100
1,500 reached against 1,200 planned: 1,500 / 1,200 x 100 = 125%
Percentage of a group
Part / whole x 100
200 of 250 replies rated it useful: 200 / 250 x 100 = 80%
Average cost per event
Total cost / number of events
Percentage increase
(New - old) / old x 100
Budget share
Total x percentage

blocks.note: Cost per enquiry or per application is only useful when compared with something: an earlier campaign, the cost of paper processing, or a target. Also look at quality: how many applications were complete and approved, not only how many were received.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: After each event, hold a short meeting of the team to discuss what worked and what did not. The main benefit is that **lessons learned are used to improve the next event**; its purpose is not to find someone to blame. Record the lessons, store the evaluation with the plan and read them when planning the next promotion.

ul: Collect feedback from visitors with a short, simple form.
Compare results with the aims and with the budget.
Say what to repeat, what to change and what to stop.
Report to the director, with figures and recommendations.
explain what the mandate, mission, vision, services and stakeholders of an organisation are, and give a 30-second summary of its work.
explain why every member of staff is an ambassador, and how conduct affects reputation.
follow brand guidelines and spot a logo or flyer that does not follow them.
stay within my brief, and say "I will find out" instead of guessing or promising.
keep to political neutrality, decline or declare gifts and declare conflicts of interest.
refuse to discuss confidential matters, such as contracts still being negotiated.
prepare key messages, a briefing note and likely questions with approved answers.
use correct titles and follow protocol, order of precedence and dress codes.
answer difficult questions calmly and refer media enquiries to the communications unit.
follow the rules for official and personal social media.
plan a booth or outreach event: aims, audience, messages, channels, budget and roles.
represent my body at a meeting, vote in line with its position and avoid commitments beyond my authority.
write a report back with outcomes, commitments and follow-up.
calculate cost per enquiry, percentage of target, percentage of replies and budget shares, and check each sum twice.

terms: Mandate
The official purpose and powers of a public body, usually given by law.
Mission statement
A short statement of an organisation's core purpose.
Reputation
How the public, partners and others see and judge an organisation.
Brand guidelines
The document that says how the logo, colours and fonts must be used.
Elevator pitch
A clear summary of the organisation's work that can be said in about 30 seconds.
Citizens' charter
A public promise of the service standards people can expect.
Key messages
The few clear points the organisation wants people to remember.
Brief
The instruction on what a representative may say and commit to.
Spokesperson
The person authorised to speak to the media for the organisation.
Political neutrality
The duty not to take sides in party politics when doing official work.
Code of conduct
The standards of behaviour expected of public officers, including rules on gifts.
Conflict of interest
Private interests that could affect, or seem to affect, official duties.
Protocol
The accepted way of treating officials and guests at formal events.
Order of precedence
The accepted order in which dignitaries are ranked, seated and introduced.
Outreach
Taking information and services out into communities.
Public relations (PR)
Managing the organisation's relationship and reputation with the public.
Cost per enquiry
Total cost of a promotion divided by the number of enquiries.

c1.title: A booth at an agricultural show
c1.text: A government agency that supports small farmers will have a booth at a three-day agricultural show near May Pen, Clarendon. The agency has J$800,000 for the booth and has set an aim of 250 serious enquiries about its input loans. The booth team is led by Marcia Reid. Visitors will include farmers, school groups and some journalists.

c2.title: A market relocation meeting
c2.text: A municipal corporation in Westmoreland plans to move vendors from a crowded street to a new market building in Savanna-la-Mar. Officer Desmond Walker is sent to a public meeting with the vendors' association. His director's brief says the move will happen, the date is not yet fixed and stall fees have not been decided. Many vendors are angry and some are shouting.

c3.title: An awards panel and a gift
c3.text: Kerry-Ann Sinclair works for an agency that promotes local manufacturers. She sits on a panel choosing the winner of a promotion award. One of the entrants is a company owned by her cousin. After a talk she gives, a contractor that supplies the agency offers her an expensive gold bracelet as a thank-you.

c4.title: Opening a health centre
c4.text: A regional health authority will open a new health centre in Black River, St Elizabeth. The Minister of Health, the Mayor and the Custos will attend. Event coordinator Paulette Grant has never organised an event with so many dignitaries. The agency's communications unit has a protocol officer.

c5.title: A journalist and a social media post
c5.text: At an agency's stand at a trade expo in Kingston, a radio reporter asks officer Rohan Edwards whether the agency's budget is about to be cut. Rohan has heard a rumour but has no facts. Earlier, a junior officer posted photos of the stand on her personal page with a comment criticising the Minister's policy.

questions.q: The agency wants a clear plan for its show booth. What should Marcia's team decide first?
o: The design of the banner and the colour of the table covers
The number of free items to give each visitor
What the booth must achieve and for whom
Which staff would most enjoy three days at the show
questions.why: Planning starts with the aim and the audience. Design, give-aways and staffing follow from them.

questions.q: The agency spends J$800,000 and records 200 serious enquiries. What is the cost per enquiry, and did it meet the aim of 250?
o: J$4,000 per enquiry; no, it reached 80% of the aim
J$4,000 per enquiry; yes, because costs stayed in budget
J$250 per enquiry; yes, because the figure is low
J$250 per enquiry; no, it reached 20% of the aim
questions.why: J$800,000 divided by 200 is J$4,000. The aim was 250, and 200 is 80% of 250, so the aim was not met even though the spending stayed within budget.

questions.q: A farmer gives his telephone number and asks for loan updates. What should the booth officer do?
o: Write it down quietly without saying what it will be used for
Tell him to phone the head office instead and not keep his number
Take it and also add his name to the agency's general mailing list
Explain why the number is wanted and note it with his consent
questions.why: Contact details are taken only with consent, for a stated purpose. Adding him to other lists goes beyond what he agreed to.

questions.q: The agency's input loans programme is for farmers with less than five hectares. Which key message is best for the leaflet?
o: The agency is the island's most dynamic and trusted partner of the whole farming community.
Farmers with under five hectares can apply for input loans at any parish office.
Our loans are designed to unlock sustainable agricultural transformation across Clarendon.
Farmers will receive a loan within one week of first showing interest in the scheme.
questions.why: A key message is short, true, plain and says what the audience can do. The last option promises something the agency has not said it can deliver.

questions.q: A vendor shouts that the corporation has never told the vendors the truth about the move. How should Desmond respond?
o: Tell the vendors that shouting will not be allowed and continue the planned presentation
Explain that stall fees are decided by other officers, so the question is not for him
Stay calm, accept their worry, state what is decided and promise a report back
Say that the vendors have had enough time already and that the move date will stand
questions.why: Calm acknowledgement keeps trust and lets him give the facts that are decided. Defensive or dismissive replies increase anger.

questions.q: A vendors' leader asks what the new stall fee will be. Fees have not been decided. What should Desmond say?
o: That fees are not yet decided, and he will take the question back and reply by a set date
That the fees will probably stay about the same, so the vendors need not worry about them
That the fees will be set after the move, so the vendors can see the new market first
That he thinks they will be higher, since the new building cost the corporation a lot
questions.why: He must not guess or hint at undecided matters. He states what is not decided, takes the question back and promises a reply.

questions.q: One vendor asks Desmond to agree now that vendors will not pay anything for the first three months. What should he do?
o: Agree, because it will calm the meeting and the director can adjust the details later
Refuse at once, since the corporation never gives free periods
Tell the vendor to discuss it privately with the Mayor after the meeting
Say the request is beyond his authority, record it and take it to the director
questions.why: A representative cannot commit the body beyond the brief. Recording the request and taking it back is honest and keeps the decision with the right person.

questions.q: After the meeting, what is the most useful thing Desmond can do?
o: Keep his notes safely filed until the director asks how the meeting went on the day
Write a report of outcomes, commitments and replies owed, and give it to his director
Tell the other officers informally what the vendors said and how they behaved
Post a short summary of the vendors' complaints on the corporation's own page
questions.why: A back-to-office report records what was said and promised, so that follow-up happens. Informal talk or public posts about a disputed meeting can cause harm.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann learns that her cousin's company is an entrant for the award. What should she do?
o: Take part but give the company a slightly lower score to be fair
Ask her cousin to withdraw the entry without giving a reason
Declare the interest and take no part in judging that award
Take part, since the other panel members will decide as well
questions.why: A conflict of interest is declared and the officer steps aside. Adjusting her scores or relying on others does not remove the conflict.

questions.q: The contractor presses Kerry-Ann to keep the gold bracelet. What is the best response?
o: Decline it politely and report the offer, as the code of conduct requires
Accept it on behalf of the agency and keep it in a drawer in her office
Accept it and tell no one, as she did not ask the contractor for it
Accept it now and offer to give it back when the contract is renewed
questions.why: A valuable gift from a supplier can influence decisions or seem to. The code of conduct requires declining or declaring it. Accepting it, even for later return, is not acceptable.

questions.q: At the awards event, a guest asks Kerry-Ann which political party has done more to support manufacturers. What should she do?
o: Give her honest opinion, since the event is held outside her normal working hours
Say which party she votes for, so that the guests know where she stands
Praise the Government of the day, since her agency is itself a public body
Politely decline to give a party view and describe what the agency offers
questions.why: Political neutrality applies whenever she is representing the agency. She explains services and does not praise or criticise any party.

questions.q: A manager asks Kerry-Ann to design a flyer for the award using the agency's logo, stretched wider and in new colours "to look fresh". What should she do?
o: Use the new look, since a fresh and different design will catch more attention
Follow the brand guidelines, and ask the communications unit about any change
Leave the logo off the flyer so that it cannot be linked to the agency's name
Use the new look on a small print run first and see how people react to it
questions.why: Corporate identity must follow the brand guidelines. Changes to the logo or colours are made by the communications unit, not by individual units.

questions.q: Paulette is unsure how to introduce the Minister, the Mayor and the Custos. What is the best step?
o: Use first names for all three guests so that the whole event feels friendly
Use the same title for all three guests, so that no one is offended by the order
Check the correct titles and order of precedence with the protocol officer first
Introduce them in the order in which they arrive at the venue on the day
questions.why: Protocol is set by accepted practice, not by guesswork or arrival order. The protocol officer can confirm titles and the order.

questions.q: Which invitation arrangement best shows good protocol?
o: Send invitations in good time with correct titles, and confirm who will attend
Send a general notice to all offices a day before the event takes place
Invite the dignitaries by telephone on the morning of the opening itself
Let each guest choose where to sit when they arrive at the health centre
questions.why: Good protocol starts early: correct titles, time to reply and clear confirmation. Seating and speaking order are then planned in advance.

questions.q: Paulette must brief the health centre's staff who will meet visitors on the day. Which staff briefing is most useful?
o: A list of the health authority's budget problems, so staff understand the pressure
A request that staff avoid talking to visitors, so that nothing wrong is said
The full history of the health centre project and of everyone who worked on it
The key services, opening times, correct titles and where to refer other questions
questions.why: Staff are ambassadors. They need the facts visitors ask about and a clear way to refer questions. Silence or internal problems do not help.

questions.q: At the opening, a resident tells Paulette that an ambulance service in her district is very slow. This is not the topic of the event. What should Paulette do?
o: Say that the event is about the new health centre, so she cannot help the resident
Record the concern, pass it to the right unit and tell the resident that she has
Promise the resident that the ambulance service will be improved within a month
Suggest that the resident writes to the newspapers about the ambulance service
questions.why: Concerns raised at an event are recorded and passed on, even when outside its topic. Promising a fix she cannot guarantee would be wrong.

questions.q: The reporter asks Rohan about the rumoured budget cut. What should Rohan do?
o: Say that he has heard the same rumour, so it is probably true and will happen
Deny it firmly, so that the visitors at the stand are not worried by the news
Refer the reporter to the communications unit, without confirming or denying it
Give his own view off the record, since it cannot then be quoted by the radio
questions.why: Only authorised persons speak to the media. Confirming a rumour or denying it without facts could mislead, and "off the record" offers no protection.

questions.q: Why is the junior officer's personal post a concern?
o: It can be read as the agency's view, and it criticises policy while she is linked to it
The photos may not be sharp enough to show the agency's stand to its best advantage
Staff are never allowed to mention their work or workplace on any personal page
Her friends may not understand what the agency does or why it was at the expo
questions.why: Officers must not present views, especially criticism of policy, in a way that can be read as the agency's. The problem is the comment, not the photos.

questions.q: After the expo, the communications unit finds 20 news stories about the agency's stand, of which 14 were positive. What is the best way to use these figures?
o: Report that 70% were positive and leave out the six that were not
Report that 14 stories is enough and file them without further reading
Report the 14 positive stories only, as the others were minor
Report that 70% were positive and read the other six for lessons
questions.why: 14 divided by 20 is 70%. An honest evaluation reports the figure and studies the negative stories to learn what to change; hiding them wastes the lesson.

questions.q: A manager wants the agency's expo poster to say "all licences in 24 hours", but the usual time is five working days. What should the officer preparing the poster do?
o: Use the claim, since nobody reads posters closely enough to check them
Raise the concern and suggest a true claim, such as five working days
Use the claim, with a note in small print about possible delays
Use the claim only on posters that are displayed outside Kingston
questions.why: Promotion must be truthful. A false promise causes complaints and harms trust, and small print does not cure it.
